events.title: Bush by thirteen
events.text: George W. Bush carried North Carolina by 12.8 points, as Republicans had in every presidential race since 1980.

events.title: Attorney General Cooper
events.text: Roy Cooper, a state senator from Nash County, took office as attorney general; he served four terms.

events.title: Dole wins Helms's seat
events.text: Elizabeth Dole beat Erskine Bowles, 53.6 to 45.0 percent, for the seat Jesse Helms had held since 1973.

events.title: Duke lacrosse
events.text: On 11 April Attorney General Cooper dropped all charges against three Duke lacrosse players, calling them innocent.

events.title: Obama carries the state
events.text: Barack Obama carried North Carolina by a third of a point, the first Democrat to do so since 1976.

events.title: Hagan beats Dole
events.text: Kay Hagan of Greensboro beat Senator Dole, 52.6 to 44.2 percent; no Democrat has won a Senate race here since.

events.title: A Republican legislature
events.text: Republicans won both houses of the General Assembly for the first time since 1870; they have held them since.

events.title: Romney by two
events.text: Mitt Romney carried North Carolina by two points.

events.title: Tillis elected
events.text: Thom Tillis, speaker of the state House, beat Senator Hagan by 1.6 points.

events.title: Governor by 10,000 votes
events.text: Roy Cooper beat Governor Pat McCrory by about 10,000 votes, the same year Donald Trump carried the state.

events.title: HB2 repeal deal
events.text: On 30 March Cooper signed the compromise repeal of HB2, the law on bathrooms and local anti-discrimination rules.

events.title: Whatley leads the state party
events.text: In June Michael Whatley, an energy lobbyist, became chairman of the North Carolina Republican Party.

events.title: Tillis re-elected
events.text: Tillis beat Cal Cunningham, 48.7 to 46.9 percent.

events.title: Cooper re-elected
events.text: Cooper beat Lieutenant Governor Dan Forest by 4.5 points as Trump carried the state by 1.3.

events.title: Prison settlement
events.text: To settle a lawsuit over COVID in the prisons, about 3,500 inmates were released early or moved to community supervision.

events.title: Unaffiliated lead
events.text: In March unaffiliated voters became the largest group on the rolls, ahead of both parties.

events.title: Budd elected
events.text: Ted Budd beat Cheri Beasley, 50.5 to 47.3 percent, for the seat of the retiring Richard Burr.

events.title: Medicaid expansion
events.text: On 27 March Cooper signed Medicaid expansion, passed by the Republican-led legislature.

events.title: Abortion veto overridden
events.text: In May the legislature overrode Cooper's veto of a 12-week limit on most abortions.

events.title: Whatley leads the RNC
events.text: On 8 March Whatley was elected chairman of the Republican National Committee.

events.title: Hurricane Helene
events.text: On 26–27 September Helene killed more than 100 people in western North Carolina; damage is put at about $60 billion.

events.title: Split tickets
events.text: Trump carried the state by 3.2 points while the Democrat Josh Stein won the governorship by 14.8.

events.title: Robeson swings
events.text: Trump won 63.4 percent in Robeson County, home of the Lumbee Tribe, up from 58.9 in 2020.

events.title: A 734-vote race
events.text: Justice Allison Riggs kept her Supreme Court seat by 734 votes after six months of challenges.

events.title: Tillis votes no
events.text: On 28 June Tillis voted against advancing the budget bill over its Medicaid cuts; the next day he said he would retire.

events.title: Lara Trump declines
events.text: On 24 July Lara Trump, a Wilmington native, said she would not run.

events.title: Cooper runs
events.text: On 28 July Roy Cooper announced his campaign by video.

events.title: Whatley runs
events.text: On 31 July Whatley launched his campaign in Gastonia, with President Trump's endorsement.

events.title: Light-rail killing
events.text: On 22 August Iryna Zarutska was killed on a Charlotte light-rail train; the killing became a theme of the campaign.

events.title: Trump in Rocky Mount
events.text: On 22 December President Trump held a rally in Rocky Mount, in Cooper's home region.

events.title: Republicans pass Democrats
events.text: In January Republican registrations passed Democratic ones for the first time.

events.title: Primary day
events.text: On 3 March Whatley won the Republican primary with 64.6 percent and Cooper the Democratic one with 92.0.

events.title: Trump in Gastonia
events.text: On 16 September President Trump held a rally for Whatley in Gastonia.

events.title: No debate
events.text: By 21 October Cooper and Whatley had not debated; Bray and Dublin debated online on 15 October.

events.title: Super PAC pauses
events.text: On 2 October the Senate Leadership Fund paused its advertising in North Carolina.

events.title: Likely Democratic
events.text: On 6 October the Cook Political Report moved the race from Lean to Likely Democratic.

events.title: Tillis backs Whatley
events.text: On 7 October Tillis said: “I support Michael Whatley and every Republican up and down the ticket.”

events.title: Early voting
events.text: In-person early voting runs from 15 October to 31 October, with same-day registration; about 924,000 ballots had been cast by 20 October, most in person.

events.title: Election Day
events.text: On 3 November polls are open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.

chartNote: Each state is coloured by the margin of the most recent presidential popular vote (Democratic minus Republican share of all votes; FEC certified results). It is a simplification: North Carolina elects its senator in its own race, and many North Carolinians split their tickets (in 2024 Donald Trump carried the state by 3.2 points while the Democrat Josh Stein won the governorship by 14.8), so the presidential colour is a backdrop, not a forecast. Shares are of land area, not of people or votes. Boundaries are today's states (Natural Earth); the map is framed on North Carolina, so outer states are cut at the edge.
